title: Trueno & Milo J Close LAMC 2026 at New York’s SummerStage & More Uplifting Moments in Latin Music
summary: Plus, the Global Impact panel explores Latin music’s worldwide reach, and Sony Latin showcases emerging artists — all in this special LAMC Edition.
contentText:
From career milestones to new releases to major announcements and those little important moments,  Billboard  editors highlight  uplifting moments  in Latin music. Here’s what happened in the Latin music world this week — LAMC (Latin Alternative Music Conference) Edition.

Trueno and Milo J Close LAMC With a Full-Capacity SummerStage Show

Trueno and Milo J closed LAMC 2026 on Saturday (Aug. 1) with a high-energy performance at Central Park’s SummerStage, where the free concert reached capacity. The Argentine artists brought two distinct but complementary visions to the stage: Trueno with his sharp, old-school rap energy, and Milo J with a soulful, genre-fluid sound rooted in the folkloric traditions of South America.

Milo J’s set stood out for its musical range and visual detail. Dressed in brown trousers and a colorful, folkloric vest, the 19-year-old artist performed songs from  La Vida Era Más Corta , including “Recordé” and “Solifican12,” backed by an ensemble featuring flute, charango and percussion galore. His dusky, intimate voice moved between rap cadences and the emotional pull of chacarera, chamamé, zamba and murga, while the crowd sang along. Later, he returned to join Trueno for “Pumas,” this time rocking a blue beanie and off-white shirt, with the duet becoming one of the night’s most memorable moments.

Trueno arrived bursting with pride, and at one point waving an Argentine flag. He performed songs from his latest album TURR4ZO , among others, leaning into the battle-rap instincts and classic hip-hop spirit that helped define his rise. His set was full of sharp flows, crowd interaction and the kind of communal energy that had fans waving flags and celebrating their roots.

Dominican rapper J Noa opened the night with a rapid-fire delivery, tightly packed verses and a confident stage presence that set the tone for the evening. Her performance brought a younger, hard-edged energy to the bill, while Argentine DJ Albina Cabrera kept the crowd moving throughout the show with a set that complemented the night’s South American focus.

Latin Music’s Global Rise Takes Center Stage

At the Global Impact of Latin Music panel on Thursday (July 30),  Billboard ’s co-chief content officer Leila Cobo moderated a conversation on the genre’s expanding global footprint, with Rosa Lagarrigue of GTS, Criteria Entertainment’s Diana Rodríguez, Glassnote Records’ Daniel Glass and PopArt’s Matías Loizaga. The panel explored how streaming, touring, festivals, local collaborations and a stronger sense of cultural identity are helping Spanish-language music reach audiences far beyond Latin America.

Cobo opened with data from Luminate’s midyear report, noting that Spanish is now the second language in global music consumption, behind English. In the U.S., one in every 10 music listeners listens to music in Spanish, even if they are not Spanish speakers. For Lagarrigue, the growth comes down in part to the emotional power of music. “People just want emotions,” she said. “They don’t need to understand the lyrics to get the emotion. They want the rhythm.”

Rodríguez pointed to the broader reach created by streaming, digital platforms and touring, noting that Latin shows are drawing increasingly diverse audiences. She said Mon Laferte’s recent U.S. tour audience was roughly 30% general-market listeners and 70% Latinos, with more diverse crowds discovering Latin artists. Loizaga added that the artists breaking through globally are “the people that get their roots and move forward with those roots,” using their culture and background to create something new.

The panelists also discussed what emerging artists need to do to break through in an increasingly crowded market. Lagarrigue emphasized patience, persistence and trying different paths, while Rodríguez advised artists to “know your voice,” identify their market, focus on one territory at a time and build gradually. Glass urged artists to prioritize direct connections with fans, even in small rooms. “If you can come back, my algorithm is: let’s play in front of 10 the week after,” he said. “I don’t care if it’s a pub or a club. Play and bond with fans, and then they will come.”

Sony Music Latin Highlights Emerging Voices at DROM

Sony Music Latin’s showcase at DROM on July 28 brought a mix of emerging artists and established momentum to the first night of LAMC after dark. Poe Leos stood out with a high-pitched vocal delivery and a corrido-trap performance that also highlighted her rapping, while Mariangela quickly connected with the crowd through her warm stage presence, accordion, electric guitar and cumbia-driven set. She also paid tribute to Selena with “La Carcacha” and to Los Tigres del Norte with “La Puerta Negra.”

The showcase continued with performances from Elena Sofía, who brought a polished pop sensibility to the stage, and YEИDRY, who shifted the mood with a soulful, stripped-down performance backed by acoustic guitar. Yk It’s Junaa and Argentine singer Luck Ra were also part of the lineup, which reflected the range of emerging voices shaping Sony Music Latin’s roster. Elena Sofía, recently featured in  Billboard ’s  On the Radar Latin , is a 17-year-old Puerto Rican singer-songwriter and multi-instrumentalist who signed with Sony Music Latin in April.

Wonder Women of Latin Music

This year, the Wonder Women of Latin Music panel, presented by Amazon, brought together a group of key women from various sectors of the industry to discuss leadership and impact.

Moderated by Billboard Español deputy editor Sigal Ratner-Arias, the event featured Tuti Bou, who currently leads Sony Music Puerto Rico; Ana Rosa Santiago, senior vice president of Latin music at Universal Music Publishing Group for the U.S. and Latin America; Chilean singer-songwriter Francisca Valenzuela, founder of the Ruidosa festival; Sandra Jiménez, regional director and head of music for YouTube in Latin America and US-Latin; Alejandra Olea, managing director of the Americas at Believe; Vicky López Borzacchini, industry relations senior manager for U.S. Latin at Amazon Music; and Claudia Ochoa, senior vice president of The Orchard Mexico.

Highlights of the discussion included the importance of initiatives such as YouTube’s Amplify-HER program, Believe’s Women in Music, and Valenzuela’s Ruidosa festival — all of which support, promote and recognize the work of women in the industry, whether as performers or in production and executive roles — as well as the need to continue opening doors and building bridges to ensure they achieve equal footing and opportunities.
